lessons.title: Lesson 1: What data annotation and micro-jobs are
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the main kinds of AI data tasks and the skill each one needs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of eight online tasks, you will identify which ones are data annotation or micro-tasks and name the skill each one needs, getting at least 6 of 8 right.
AI tools learn from examples. People prepare those examples by adding labels: this photo shows a bicycle, this message is a complaint, this sentence is in Hausa, this AI answer is better than that one. Adding labels is called data annotation or data labeling.
Common task types: image labeling (drawing a box around each car, or choosing a category), text labeling (is this review positive, negative or neutral?), audio work (typing what a speaker says, or recording your own voice reading sentences), and AI response rating (reading two answers from an AI and choosing the better one, with a reason). Some newer projects ask for experts, such as nurses, accountants or people who speak two languages well.
Micro-jobs are small online tasks paid one at a time, often taking seconds to minutes. Some people do them on open platforms from home; others are hired as employees in an office, for example by companies with data teams in Nairobi or Kampala. Either way, the key skills are careful reading, following rules exactly, steady attention and honesty.
Words to know:
- Data annotation (data labeling): adding labels to photos, text, audio or video so an AI tool can learn from them.
- Micro-job (micro-task): a small online task, paid one at a time.
- AI response rating: reading answers from an AI tool and judging which is better, using rules.
- Transcription: typing out exactly what is said in a recording.
Official sources:
- Sama careers (offices in Nairobi, Kenya, and Gulu and Kampala, Uganda)
- ILO: The role of digital labour platforms in transforming the world of work
Try it now: Write the four task types (image, text, audio, AI rating) on paper. Next to each, write one skill you already have that fits it, for example "I speak English and Twi" next to audio, or "I notice small details" next to images.
You can now name the main kinds of AI data tasks and match each to a skill you already have.

check.q: Which of these is a data annotation task?
options: Selling phones online
Delivering food on a motorbike
Drawing a box around every car in a street photo
Repairing a laptop screen
check.why: Drawing boxes around objects is image labeling, one of the main annotation tasks.

check.q: A task shows you two AI answers and asks which is better and why. What kind of task is it?
options: AI response rating
Transcription
Image labeling
Data entry of invoices
check.why: Judging AI answers with a reason is AI response rating.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Labeling by the guideline
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Label ten sample items by following a written guideline and flag the unclear ones.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short labeling guideline and ten sample items, you will label each item by following the guideline and flag the unclear ones, matching the answer key on at least 8 of 10.
Every project has a guideline: the rules for how to label. It says what each label means, gives examples, and explains the hard cases. Your opinion does not matter as much as the guideline. If the guideline says "a person on a poster counts as a person", you label it, even if it feels strange.
Read the whole guideline before your first task, then keep it open. Look for the examples and the edge cases: the items that could fit two labels. Most mistakes happen there.
When an item is truly unclear, do not guess wildly. Use the skip or flag option if there is one, or follow what the guideline says to do with unclear items. Careful and consistent beats fast.
Step by step:
- Read the whole guideline once, slowly.
- Write down each label and its meaning in your own words.
- Study the examples and the edge cases.
- Label each item, checking the guideline when you are not sure.
- Flag or skip items the guideline does not cover, as it tells you to.
Words to know:
- Guideline: the written rules for a labeling project: what each label means and how to handle hard cases.
- Edge case: an item that could fit more than one label, so the rule must be checked.
- Flag: mark an item as unclear or broken so a reviewer can look at it.
Try it now: Practice on paper. Guideline: label each message POSITIVE (happy with the service), NEGATIVE (unhappy) or NEUTRAL (a question or fact); if it is both happy and unhappy, label it by the main request. Label these ten: 1 "Thank you, delivery was fast!" 2 "Where is your shop in Kumasi?" 3 "The bread was stale again." 4 "Great price, but the box was broken. Please replace it." 5 "Open on Sunday?" 6 "Best tailor in Dakar!" 7 "I waited two hours." 8 "Order 2231 arrived." 9 "Love it, but I need a refund for the second one." 10 "asdf". Answer key: 1 POS, 2 NEU, 3 NEG, 4 NEG, 5 NEU, 6 POS, 7 NEG, 8 NEU, 9 NEG, 10 flag (not a real message).
You can now read a labeling guideline, apply it to each item, and flag the items it does not cover.

check.q: The guideline says a cartoon person counts as a person. You think it should not. What do you do?
options: Follow your own opinion
Label it as a person, as the guideline says
Skip every cartoon
Ask a friend on WhatsApp to decide
check.why: In labeling work, the guideline decides, not personal opinion.

check.q: An item does not fit any label in the guideline. What is the best move?
options: Pick a label at random to save time
Give it the most common label
Leave the platform
Flag or skip it as the guideline tells you
check.why: Flagging unclear items keeps the data clean and protects your quality score.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Qualification tests and quality scores
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the steps you will take to pass a qualification test and keep your quality score high.
This lesson builds toward: Before you start a qualification test, you will list the steps you will take to read the guideline, practice and check your own work, so you can explain how you will keep your quality score high.
Most projects start with a qualification test: a short set of practice tasks with known answers. You usually need a good result to get paid work. On many platforms this test time is not paid, so prepare well and take it when you are rested.
After you start, the platform keeps checking your work. Some items have hidden known answers, and reviewers check samples. Together these make your quality score. A high score can bring more tasks; a low score can remove you from a project.
To keep quality high: read any feedback, reread the guideline when it changes, slow down on edge cases, take breaks, and never use tricks or copy answers. Some projects do not allow AI tools to do the task for you; follow the project's rules.
Step by step:
- Read the guideline fully before the test.
- Do any practice tasks offered.
- Take the test when you are rested, with steady internet.
- After each batch, read the feedback and note your mistakes.
- Reread the guideline whenever it is updated.
Words to know:
- Qualification test: a short test of practice tasks you must pass before you get paid work on a project.
- Quality score: a measure of how often your labels are right, used to decide whether you get more tasks.
- Gold question: a hidden task with a known answer, used to check your accuracy.
Try it now: Mark your ten practice labels from the last lesson against the answer key. Write your score out of 10, the items you got wrong, and one rule you will check more carefully next time. Then write your five-step plan for your first real qualification test.
You can now prepare for a qualification test, check your own work against an answer key and explain how you will keep your quality score high.

check.q: What is a qualification test on a labeling project?
options: A short set of practice tasks you must pass before paid work
A school exam you pay for
A loan application
A video interview with the client's boss
check.why: Projects use a qualification test to check you can follow the guideline before giving paid tasks.

check.q: Your quality score drops after a guideline update. What should you do first?
options: Work faster to make up for it
Open a second account
Reread the updated guideline and your feedback
Ignore it; scores do not matter
check.why: Score drops after an update usually mean a rule changed; rereading it and the feedback fixes the cause.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Working safely and earning honestly

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Checking a platform is real and refusing fake jobs
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check whether a platform or job offer is real and name the warning signs of a fake one.
This lesson builds toward: Given a platform or a job offer, you will check that it is real and name any fake-job warning signs, before you pay anything or share any documents.
Real platforms exist. Examples that say on their own sites that joining is free include Appen's CrowdGen, Mindrift (where Toloka's tasks have moved) and Clickworker. Platforms change, close and accept different countries, so always check the platform's own website for your country, the work on offer and how pay is sent.
Fake "AI jobs" are everywhere, on WhatsApp, Telegram, TikTok and Facebook. The biggest sign: they ask you to pay. A real job never asks you to pay a fee to join, to unlock tasks, for training, for a starter kit or to withdraw your earnings. The US Federal Trade Commission says honest employers do not charge you to get a job.
Other warning signs: pay that sounds too good for easy work; a recruiter who only talks on WhatsApp or Telegram; tasks like liking videos or rating products where you must deposit money (often crypto) to continue; being paid and then asked to send part of it back; requests for your ID, bank PIN or one-time code in a chat; and pressure to decide today.
Step by step:
- Find the platform's official website yourself; do not use the link in the message.
- Check that joining is free and read its pay and payment pages.
- Check that it accepts workers from your country.
- Search the platform's name with the word "scam" and read what others report.
- Refuse any offer that asks you to pay, deposit or send money back.
Words to know:
- Task scam: a fake job where you do simple tasks, see fake earnings, and are told to deposit money to continue or withdraw.
- Recruiter: a person who finds workers for a company. Real ones do not charge you.
- Official website: the platform's own site, which you find yourself, not through a link someone sends you.
Official sources:
- CrowdGen by Appen (contributor projects; says it never asks you to pay to join)
- Mindrift (AI training tasks; says Toloka tasks moved here and joining is free)
- Clickworker (microtasks such as AI training data, surveys and voice recordings)
- US Federal Trade Commission: Job scams
Try it now: Pick two platforms (from this lesson, or one a friend uses). For each, write: the official website you found yourself, whether joining is free, whether it accepts your country, how pay is sent, and anything you found when you searched its name with "scam". Then write your scam stop-list of five warning signs.
You can now check a platform on its own website and refuse a fake job by naming its warning signs.

check.q: A WhatsApp message offers "AI rating work" but asks for a $20 activation fee. What is this?
options: A normal start-up cost
A fair training fee
A warning sign of a scam: real jobs never charge you to start
A tax payment
check.why: Asking you to pay to start is the clearest sign of a fake job.

check.q: How should you open a platform you heard about?
options: Click the link in the recruiter's message
Find its official website yourself and read its pages
Ask the recruiter to send screenshots
Download a file the recruiter sends
check.why: Finding the site yourself avoids fake look-alike pages and harmful files.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Protecting your data and the task data
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three rules that keep your own details and the task data private.
This lesson builds toward: While you do tasks, you will keep your own private details and the task data private, sharing no passwords, codes or task content outside the platform.
Protect yourself. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-step sign-in. Never share a one-time code, PIN or password with anyone, even someone who says they are from the platform. Real platforms may ask for ID to verify you, but only inside their official site or app, never in a chat.
Protect the data you see. Tasks can show people's photos, voices, messages or medical and money details. Many projects make you agree to keep tasks confidential. Never screenshot tasks, post them in groups, or paste them into other AI tools unless the project allows it. Countries have data protection laws and regulators, for example the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.
Protect your account. Do not share or sell your account, and do not let someone else work on it. Platforms can close accounts for this, and you may lose unpaid earnings. Use only your own real identity.
Step by step:
- Use a strong, unique password and two-step sign-in.
- Share ID only inside the platform's official site or app.
- Never share codes, PINs or passwords.
- Keep task content inside the platform: no screenshots or sharing.
- Never share, rent or sell your account.
Words to know:
- Two-step sign-in: a second check, like a code sent to your phone, when you sign in.
- Confidential: private: you must not share it with anyone outside the work.
- One-time code: a short code sent to you to confirm it is really you. Never share it.
Official sources:
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission
Try it now: Write your three data-safety rules in your own words: one for your account, one for your ID and codes, and one for the task data. Then turn on two-step sign-in for your email account if it is not on yet.
You can now keep your own details safe and keep the task data private.

check.q: Someone says they are platform support and asks for the code just sent to your phone. What do you do?
options: Never share it, and contact support through the official site
Send it, because support needs it
Send half of the code
Post it in a group to ask
check.why: One-time codes are only for you; sharing one lets someone take over your account.

check.q: A task shows a photo of a stranger's medical letter. What is right?
options: Screenshot it for practice
Share it in your study group
Paste it into a free AI tool to read it
Label it inside the platform and share it with no one
check.why: Task data is confidential and stays inside the platform.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Working out your real pay and making a plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record your time and pay and work out your real hourly earnings.
This lesson builds toward: After a week of practice or real tasks, you will record your time and pay and work out your real hourly earnings, counting unpaid time such as tests and searching for tasks.
Pay for micro-jobs is uneven. It differs by project, country and platform; some weeks there are many tasks and some weeks none. Time on tests, training and searching for tasks is often unpaid. The International Labour Organization has studied platform work and calls for it to be decent work, with fair pay and conditions.
So measure it. Keep a log of every session: date, minutes worked (including tests and waiting), tasks done, and money earned. Real hourly pay = total money earned ÷ total hours, counting all the time. Example: you earned 6 dollars in a week and spent 4 hours in total, so your real hourly pay is 1.50 dollars.
Then decide. Compare it with other options near you. Many people treat micro-work as extra income or a first step toward better-paid roles, such as quality reviewer, expert projects, or a full-time job at a data company. Keep records of what you are paid, and ask your national tax authority whether and how to declare it.
Step by step:
- Log each session: date, total minutes (with tests and waiting), tasks, money.
- Add up the week's money and the week's hours.
- Divide money by hours to get your real hourly pay.
- Compare it with your other options.
- Plan next month: hours, platforms, and one skill to grow.
Words to know:
- Real hourly pay: all the money you earned divided by all the hours you spent, including unpaid time.
- Unpaid time: time on tests, training and searching for tasks that earns nothing.
- Log: a simple written record you fill in each time you work.
Official sources:
- ILO: The role of digital labour platforms in transforming the world of work
Try it now: Draw a log with five columns: date, minutes (all of them), tasks, money, notes. Fill one row from today's practice (money 0). Then write a 4-week plan with dates: which two platforms you will check or join, how many hours a week, and the day each week you will work out your real hourly pay.
You can now keep a time-and-pay log, work out your real hourly pay and plan your next four weeks.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Practice labels Fewer than 8 of 10 match the key, or unclear items were guessed. At least 8 of 10 match the key and the unclear item is flagged. 10 of 10, with a one-page guideline in your own words that covers the edge cases. Test and quality plan No plan, or the plan is only "work fast". Five steps: read the guideline, practice, test rested, read feedback, reread updates. Also lists your own mistakes from practice and the rule you will check for each. Platforms checked A platform was chosen from a link in a message, or a fee was accepted. Two platforms checked on official sites: free to join, your country, how pay is sent. Also includes a scam search for each and a five-sign scam stop-list in your own words. Data-safety rules Rules are missing, or the plan shares codes, ID or task data in a chat. Three clear rules: account, ID and codes, and task data. Two-step sign-in is turned on and the rules say what to do if someone asks for a code. Pay log and plan No log, or the log counts only paid time. A log that counts all minutes, the real hourly pay formula, and a 4-week plan with dates. Also compares the result with another option and names one skill to grow for better-paid work. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: You earned 10 dollars and spent 5 hours in total, including 1 unpaid test hour. What is your real hourly pay?
options: 10 dollars an hour
2.50 dollars an hour
2 dollars an hour
5 dollars an hour
check.why: Real hourly pay counts all the time: 10 dollars ÷ 5 hours = 2 dollars an hour.

check.q: What should your work log include?
options: Only the money you earned
Only the days you were paid
Your password, so you remember it
Date, all minutes including tests and waiting, tasks and money
check.why: Counting every minute and every payment shows what the work really pays.
